steps.body: A **dot plot** turns a data set into a picture: a number line for the possible values, one **dot per data value**, stacked when values repeat. The pets data 0,1,1,2,2,2,3,4 becomes stacks of height 1,2,3,1,1 — eight dots for eight students, and the tallest stack (at 2) shows the most common answer at a glance.
Each dot is one data point. Stack the dots above each value to build the plot — the tallest stack marks the most common answer.

widget.prompt: Build the dot plot: 1 student read 0 books, 3 read 1, 4 read 2, 2 read 3.
widget.successFeedback: Every stack matches — the peak at 2 books is the most common result.
widget.partialFeedback: Some stacks are the wrong height. Each dot is one student — count them from the data.

predict.prompt: Before you build it: which number of books will have the tallest stack of dots?
predict.reveal: Four students read 2 books — more than any other count — so 2 gets the tallest stack. The tallest stack in a dot plot is the mode: the most common value.

cml.actionGoal: Build and inspect a distribution while coordinating individual values, center, spread, and shape.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: Move one extreme value farther away. Which measures should change, and which might stay stable?

explanation.prompt: Why must a claim about a distribution use more than its center?

options.label: Spread and shape can differ even when centers match.
options.feedback: Exactly. A distribution is determined by the pattern of all its values.

options.label: The mean alone completely describes every dataset.
options.feedback: That describes a surface feature, not the mathematical relationship that must remain true. A distribution is determined by the pattern of all its values.

widget.prompt: In the pets dot plot, how many students have exactly 2 pets? (Count the dots above 2.)

commonErrors.feedback: 2 is the VALUE on the number line, not the count of dots above it. Count the stack: 3 dots = 3 students.
8 is ALL the dots (every student). The question asks only about the stack above 2: 3 dots.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Three dots sit above 2, so 3 students have 2 pets.

explanationVariants: 1+2+3+1+1 = 8 dots — one per student, so 8 students were surveyed.
The dot count always equals the data-set size.

widget.prompt: Add up ALL the dots in the pets plot (stacks of 1, 2, 3, 1, 1). How many students does the plot show?

commonErrors.feedback: 5 counts the STACKS (distinct values 0-4), not the dots. Each dot is one student: 1+2+3+1+1 = 8.
10 adds the VALUES on the number line (0+1+2+3+4). Count the DOTS instead: 8.

steps.body: Building a dot plot has just two moves: draw a number line covering the smallest to largest value, then place one dot per data value, **stacking upward on repeats**. Nothing is lost — you can recover the entire data set by reading the dots back.

widget.prompt: The data is 1, 2, 2, 3. Build the dot plot: stack 1 dot in the '1' column, 2 dots in the '2' column (from the bottom), and 1 dot in the '3' column.

pointErrors.feedback: A third dot at 2 would mean THREE students answered 2 — the data has only two 2s.
A second dot at 1 would mean two students answered 1 — the data has only one.

widget.missFeedback: One dot per data value: the value 1 appears once, 2 appears twice (stack them), 3 appears once.
widget.successFeedback: Built — four dots for four data values, with the repeat at 2 stacked.

cml.actionGoal: Place ordered pairs and coordinate each observation across two quantitative variables.

explanationVariants: Stacks of 2,3,2,1 over the values 10,15,20,25 read back as 10,10,15,15,15,20,20,25.
Each dot converts back to one data value — the plot IS the data.

widget.prompt: A dot plot shows 2 dots over 10, 3 over 15, 2 over 20, and 1 over 25. Which data set does it show?

options.feedback: Right — each dot reads back as one value: two 10s, three 15s, two 20s, one 25.
That lists each value ONCE, ignoring the stack heights. The stacks say how many times each value occurred.
Those are the stack HEIGHTS (the counts), not the data values themselves. The values are on the number line: 10s, 15s, 20s, 25.

hints: Each dot is one data value.
The number line gives the value; the stack gives how many.

explanationVariants: An empty spot above a value means NO student gave that answer — a count of zero.
Gaps are real information: that value simply didn't occur.

widget.prompt: A dot plot of quiz scores has no dots above 7. What does that mean?

options.label: No student scored 7
options.feedback: Right — an empty column is a count of zero for that value.

options.label: The value 7 was impossible
options.feedback: 7 was possible (it's on the number line) — it just didn't OCCUR. Empty column = zero count.

options.label: The plot has an error
options.feedback: Gaps are normal and informative — they show which values never appeared in the data.

hints: "More than 15 minutes" means the stacks above 20 and 25.
explanationVariants: Values above 15 are 20 (2 dots) and 25 (1 dot): 3 students read more than 15 minutes.
Count only the stacks strictly right of 15: 2 + 1 = 3.

widget.prompt: In the reading plot (2 dots over 10, 3 over 15, 2 over 20, 1 over 25), how many students read MORE than 15 minutes?

commonErrors.feedback: 6 includes the three students AT 15 — but "more than 15" is strict, excluding them: 2 + 1 = 3.
2 counts only the 20-minute stack, missing the student at 25: 2 + 1 = 3.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Strictly more than 15: the stacks at 20 (2) and 25 (1): 3 students.

steps.body: One dot per value, stacked on repeats.
takeaways: A dot plot puts one dot per data value above a number line, stacking repeats.
Total dots = data-set size; stack height = that value's count; gaps = zero counts.
The plot loses nothing — the whole data set reads back from the dots.
steps.teaser: next: when data gets big, bars replace dots — histograms.

concept.body: Quick rewind. **Stack height = how many times that value occurred.** Data 5,5,6: two dots stack above 5, one dot above 6 — three dots for three values.

explanationVariants: The value 5 occurred twice, so its stack is 2 dots tall.
Stack height equals that value's count in the data.

widget.prompt: For the data 5, 5, 6, how many dots stack above the value 5?

commonErrors.feedback: 5 is the VALUE, not its count. The value 5 appears twice in the data: 2 dots.
3 is the whole data set's size. Only the two 5s stack above 5; the 6 gets its own column.

widget.fallbackFeedback: The data holds two 5s: 2 dots above 5.
